clue.text: Spirit photograph that takes the biscuit?

blocks.note: brandy is a spirit distilled from wine
a snap is a casual photograph

explanation.surface: A snapshot of a drink so remarkable that it beats everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes the biscuit' is the idiom for being the most outrageous, but here the biscuit is simply the thing being defined.
explanation.definitionFit: A brandy snap is a thin, crisp rolled biscuit flavoured with ginger, often filled with cream.

clue.text: The sort of speech that gets reported

definitions.text: The sort of speech that gets reported

blocks.clueFragment: The sort of speech that gets reported
blocks.note: surface reading: the kind of public address journalists write up
setter's reading: the grammatical term for speech given second-hand, as in 'he said that...'

explanation.walkthrough: Grammar books call it reported speech, the form used when quoting someone without their exact words.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammarians use this term for speech relayed second-hand rather than quoted in the speaker's exact words.

blocks.note: to be off is to be leaving
the tip of something is its end

explanation.surface: Someone causes offence by walking out without tipping the waiter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaving a tip' sounds like a gratuity; read it as two pieces, leaving and a tip.
explanation.definitionFit: To insult someone is to hurt their feelings, the same as giving offence to them.

blocks.note: surface reading: something determined to make others submit
setter's reading: the leg joint that bends when someone goes down to the floor in homage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent on' looks like the idiom for determined; here it is literal bending, as when kneeling before a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: Kneeling to show submission or deference means bending this leg joint down to the ground.

blocks.note: surface reading: a man with a crafty expression
setter's reading: a man who looks slyly, secretly watching others

explanation.walkthrough: The legend of Lady Godiva gives the name to the tailor who spied on her, now a term for any voyeur.
explanation.definitionFit: A voyeur who secretly spies on others is named after the tailor who peeped at Lady Godiva.

blocks.note: surface reading: arrives at just the right moment
setter's reading: an arrival recorded by a time clock at work

explanation.walkthrough: Workers once punched a card in a time clock on arriving, so their entrance is literally timed.
explanation.definitionFit: Workers register their arrival by stamping a card in a time clock, recording the moment they start work.

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the word is only one possible arrangement, so its letters may be reordered

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A romance that ties two people together, maybe a marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A binding affair' reads as a commitment; the binding is a material and the affair is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Raffia is palm-leaf fibre used by gardeners and craftspeople to tie things, so it serves as a binding material.

indicators.note: only a part of the preceding word is wanted, a run of letters within it

blocks.note: the second to fifth letters of this word

explanation.surface: An instruction to observe a portion of the ear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of the ear' looks like the definition, but 'part' signals the hidden word and only 'of the ear' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Otic is the medical adjective relating to hearing anatomy, from the Greek word for ear.

clue.text: Telephone receiver will provide a form of protection

blocks.note: to ring someone is to telephone them
a fence is a receiver of stolen goods

explanation.surface: A telephone handset somehow offers its user a kind of safeguard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Telephone receiver' reads as the handset; split it into a verb and a criminal receiver.
explanation.definitionFit: Ring-fencing guarantees that funds or assets are kept apart and protected from other uses.

indicators.note: to speak means we take the sound of the next word, not its spelling

blocks.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' looks like speed but is the noun for a period of abstinence; Lent is the forty days before Easter.
explanation.definitionFit: Leant is the past tense of lean, describing something tilted or sloping at an angle.

indicators.note: in tells us one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: the contraction I've
split as in + nate: the first two letters signal the insertion and the remainder is the outer piece

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to a born simplicity of character.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter splits a single word in two, a rare trick: its front half is the insertion signal, its back half the letters around the contraction.
explanation.definitionFit: Naivety is innocent simplicity and lack of guile, the same quality as artlessness.

blocks.note: first meaning: peaceful, tranquil
second meaning: the largest ocean on Earth

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a description of still water; the explorer Magellan named the ocean for its peacefulness.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means peaceable, and the noun names the vast ocean between Asia and the Americas.

blocks.note: surface reading: crack or cave in when stressed
setter's reading: surrender or concede, as to traffic or to an argument

explanation.walkthrough: The traffic sign for giving way to other road users uses this same word in the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: To yield is to submit or concede, whether to an opponent's argument or to oncoming traffic.

clue.text: But players may be seated here in the park

definitions.text: players may be seated here in the park

blocks.clueFragment: But players may be seated here in the park
blocks.note: surface reading: a spot in the park where sportsmen might sit

blocks.clueFragment: But players may be seated here
blocks.note: setter's reading: the 'but' points to a name that suggests standing, though musicians sit in it

explanation.walkthrough: The 'But' is the joke: the structure's name says the band stands, yet the musicians usually sit.
explanation.definitionFit: This roofed outdoor platform in a park is where a brass band performs concerts to the public.

clue.text: Where publicans may be locked up

definitions.text: Where publicans may be locked up

blocks.clueFragment: Where publicans may be locked up
blocks.note: surface reading: the prison cells where innkeepers are held
setter's reading: publicans work at the back of the counters in their pubs

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means in prison, but a publican literally spends the day standing at the back of the pub counter.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means imprisoned, while publicans literally serve drinks from the far side of their counters.

clue.text: He is used to holding the lead

definitions.text: He is used to holding the lead

blocks.clueFragment: He is used to holding the lead
blocks.note: surface reading: a habitual front-runner in a race
setter's reading: gripping a leash attached to an animal

explanation.walkthrough: 'Holding the lead' suggests being in first place; the lead is a leash, as held by police officers with trained animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Police and security officers who work with trained animals keep them under control on a leash.

clue.text: Offering no resistance all the same

blocks.note: first meaning: read as two words, failing to stand up against something
second meaning: nevertheless, in spite of that

explanation.walkthrough: Split as 'not withstanding', it describes a lack of resistance; as one word it means nevertheless.
explanation.definitionFit: Read whole, the word is a formal adverb meaning nevertheless or in spite of this.

clue.text: Cat Enid and I groomed for show

indicators.note: grooming tidies and rearranges, so these letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: the words taken as written; 'and' merely joins them

explanation.surface: Enid prepares her cat for exhibiting at a cat show, with the speaker's help.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show' looks like a noun for a pet contest, but it is a verb defining the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To indicate something is to point it out or make it plain, which is what showing does.

blocks.note: first meaning: literally put into a sack
second meaning: certain, as good as won

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacked' suggests dismissal from a job; take it literally as placed inside a sack.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a result that is secured and certain, like a catch already stowed in a sack.

blocks.note: surface reading: a sham candidacy for an award or office
setter's reading: a false name, nomination taken as naming

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nomination' usually means putting someone forward; here it is literally a naming.
explanation.definitionFit: A pen name or alias adopted to hide a writer's real identity is a false name.

clue.text: Gloss over title in the Spanish style

indicators.note: in places the first piece inside the second

blocks.note: a title is the name of something
el is the Spanish word for the

explanation.surface: Someone skates over an honorific given in the manner of Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gloss over' looks like the idiom for hiding faults; 'Gloss' alone defines, a glossy coating.
explanation.definitionFit: Enamel is a hard shiny coating or paint, so it provides a gloss on a surface.

clue.text: Run out of pictures to back

indicators.note: going to the back means the word is read from its end to its start

blocks.note: ex means out of or former
pictures are works of art

explanation.surface: Someone has run out of photographs to support a project.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a run not scored off the bat, such as a bye or wide, is called an extra.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, runs given away by byes, wides and no-balls are counted as extras in the score.

blocks.note: first meaning: any of the English kings of that name
second meaning: the first name of the nonsense poet Lear

explanation.walkthrough: King Lear is Shakespeare's tragic monarch, but here Lear is the Victorian nonsense poet, whose forename is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Eight English monarchs bore this name, as did the author of 'The Owl and the Pussycat'.

blocks.note: surface reading: a grizzling, whining baby
setter's reading: the young of a grizzly, a North American species

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grizzly' sounds like grizzly, the British word for a crying, fretful child; it is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The young of a large brown North American animal is called a cub, as with lions and foxes.

blocks.note: first meaning: cheer up
second meaning: to jump or leap suddenly, as a startled horse does

explanation.walkthrough: 'Please start' reads as a polite request to begin; both words are verbs with separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Being bucked by news means being pleased by it, and a horse that bucks starts or jumps up.

blocks.note: surface reading: a tidy servant or waiter
setter's reading: neat is an old word for cattle, so this attends to cattle

explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' looks like tidy, but it is an archaic word for cattle; 'neat's-foot oil' preserves it.
explanation.definitionFit: A person employed to tend grazing cattle is their keeper, the attendant of a herd.

blocks.note: surface reading: good sense, as in having a head on one's shoulders
setter's reading: a headland, and also a garment worn on the shoulders

explanation.walkthrough: It sounds like the idiom for sensible; the word means both a headland and a sleeveless cloak.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a coastal headland and a sleeveless cloak worn over the shoulders.

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
the Labour Party sits on the political left

explanation.surface: A split between Britain's two major political parties.
explanation.walkthrough: Conservative and Labour are Britain's main right- and left-wing parties.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleft is a split or fissure, like the crack that a rift opens in rock.

clue.text: Journalist's work needs to be bang on time

blocks.note: a report is a loud bang, as of a gun
an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A journalist's copy must be delivered exactly to deadline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bang on time' looks like the idiom for punctual; split it, with 'on' simply joining two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Reportage is the reporting of news by the press, the typical output of a correspondent.
